newsitem.title: USA: PSA urges bar association to adopt pay-to-play ban.
newsitem.headline: PSA urges bar association to adopt pay-to-play ban.

text.p: Municipal bond dealers this week will urge the American Bar Association to adopt a "pay-to- play" ban for bond lawyers nationwide, a spokesperson for dealers said.

Heather Ruth, president of PSA The Bond Market Trade Association, said her group will send a letter to ABA officials by Friday asking them to adopt a policy similar to a rule enacted in 1994 for bond dealers by the Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board.

Ruth outlined the plan at a forum sponsored by the Association of the Bar of the City of New York, which recently adopted a pay-to-play ban similar to MSRB's and is urging ABA and state and local bar associations nationwide to do the same.
Pay to play refers to the practice of bond professionals making contributions to elected municipal officials in return for bond business or a crack at bond business.

The City bar's rule would prohibit muni bond lawyers who make contributions to municipal clients or solicit them on behalf of clients - including so-called soft-money contributions - from engaging in bond business for two years with those governments.
The rule is modeled after MSRB's pay-to-play rule, although the board's rule does not explicity bar soft-money contributions like payments to political parties.
The City bar on March 10 urged the New York State Administrative Board, which sets standards for the state's lawyers, to adopt the rule.

The group also wants ABA to endorse the plan at its annual meeting in August. But some key ABA leaders staunchly oppose the city bar's rule. And no other city or state bar association outside of New York has endorsed it to date.

"We are not going to pretend to tell ABA precisely what to do," said Ruth, whose group helped bond dealers craft a voluntary ban on pay-to-play in 1994. The ban, which is tougher than rule G-37, remains in effect.

"We are just going to say that we think an approach like G-37 should also be applied to bond counsel, because our interest is in the integrity and reputation of the business," Ruth said. "This business continues to get slammed" in the press, she said. "Something that's applicable just to dealers won't do the whole job," she added.

Ruth said PSA's letter may not specifically refer to the New York City bar's policy. "I'm not sure we are going to reference the New York one, or just make a more general statement (that they need to) deal with it at the national level," she said.
